title: Gavi Says New TB Vaccines From 2029 Could Save 7.3 Million Lives
excerpt: Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, says novel tuberculosis vaccines expected from 2029 could avert up to 7.3 million deaths by 2050 and unlock $135 billion in economic benefits — if supply reaches the countries that need them most.
body:
• New tuberculosis vaccines are expected to become available from 2029, and Gavi estimates they could avert up to 7.3 million deaths between 2030 and 2050.
  • The vaccines could unlock up to $135 billion in economic benefits across low- and middle-income countries, according to the analysis.
  • Demand could average 86 million vaccination courses a year, but financing gaps, demand uncertainty, and manufacturer capacity could slow the rollout.
  • BCG, the only currently licensed TB vaccine, is more than a century old and its protection wanes; new candidates target adolescents and adults.

New tuberculosis vaccines expected from 2029 could avert up to 7.3 million deaths by 2050, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, said on Sept. 14 — while warning that governments and manufacturers must prepare now to secure supply.

According to the analysis published alongside Gavi's Early Market Shaping Roadmap for novel TB vaccines, demand among low- and middle-income countries could average 86 million vaccination courses per year, with greater demand in the early years as high-burden countries expand protection across multiple age groups in high-risk areas. The modelling also estimates up to $135 billion in economic benefits across those countries by mid-century, making the new vaccines potentially one of the most impactful immunization tools in decades.

"Novel TB vaccines could be the next blockbuster immunisation tool, however they will only realise their potential if we are able to ensure sufficient, predictable and affordable supply for those countries with the highest disease burden."

— Dr Sania Nishtar, CEO, Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance

Context & Background

Tuberculosis remains the world's leading infectious killer, claiming an estimated 1.23 million lives in 2024, according to World Health Organization figures. The only licensed vaccine, Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG), is more than 100 years old: it protects infants and young children against severe forms of the disease, but its protection wanes with age, leaving adolescents and adults exposed. The new candidates are designed to prevent infectious pulmonary TB among adolescents and adults — precisely the gap BCG cannot fill.

The 7.3-million-lives estimate rests on preliminary modelling by the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, which assumes 50 percent efficacy against TB disease regardless of previous exposure, with immunity waning over 10 years, in a scenario targeting high-risk populations and adolescents through routine immunization and targeted catch-up campaigns. Separately, WHO-commissioned modelling suggests that a 50-percent-effective adolescent-and-adult vaccine, if approved and rapidly scaled, could avert up to 76 million TB cases, 8.5 million deaths, and 42 million courses of antibiotics over 25 years.

Impact & Analysis

The real risk, Gavi warns, is access rather than science. Its analysis flags inadequate global and domestic financing, demand uncertainty, limited manufacturer capacity for late-stage candidates, and gaps in evidence as the risks that could slow introduction once licenses are secured. Demand uncertainty, in particular, can deter manufacturers from investing in production capacity — creating the very supply shortfalls that would hit high-burden countries first.

Several high-burden countries hosting trials are already preparing for eventual rollout. In June 2026, health officials from Kenya, Malawi, and Zambia joined more than 80 TB vaccine stakeholders at a WHO workshop in Nairobi to map implementation plans, making them among the global frontrunners preparing to introduce a new class of adult and adolescent TB vaccines. Gavi says it will continue working with partners through the WHO TB Vaccine Accelerator's Finance and Access Working Group to push for rapid, equitable access, focusing on competitive and geographically diverse manufacturing.

Diaspora Angle

India carries the world's largest tuberculosis burden by WHO estimates, so the question of who gets doses — and at what price — will land directly on Indian health systems and families, including the millions of Indian-origin households with relatives in high-burden states.

What's Next

The first of the new and promising candidate vaccines is expected to secure regulatory approval by the end of the decade. Gavi says it has begun working with partners now — years ahead of licensure — to lay the groundwork for timely access: predictable supply commitments, routine immunization programs paired with targeted catch-up campaigns, and a manufacturing pipeline spread across high-burden regions so no single supplier can become a bottleneck.
